$comment: Asset Hunter vertical atlas — the seed content source of truth. scripts/build-seed.mjs composes this into seed/seed.json, which EmDash inlines. Edit here, then run `npm run seed:build`. JSON rather than JS so the file cannot break the generator with quoting. Honesty rules: every representative is a plate generated for this catalogue, so representative_origin is always `generated`; example_count is 1 (the plate) and distinct_sources is 0 until the hunt engine supplies real observations. Unverified counts are never invented.

possibilities.title: Health you read off the world, not off a bar
possibilities.tagline: Damage as cracked glass instead of a red rectangle
possibilities.summary: Replace the health bar with a surface that degrades. The player infers remaining health from the condition of the thing they are already looking at — a visor that cracks, armour that dents, a screen that desaturates. Costs the player nothing to read, because the information arrives inside an image they are already attending to.
possibilities.technique: Layer a damage-state overlay on a first-person frame. Three discrete states (intact / hairline / breached) rather than a continuous fill, so the state is legible at a glance and at any resolution. Pair the overlay with a colour shift the player never has to be told about.
possibilities.rightsNote: The technique is free to use. Any specific visor or crack texture is reference-only until its licence is verified — discovery of a possibility never grants rights to the source asset.
possibilities.buildNotes: Three-state overlay beats a continuous fill for readability: it survives small screens, it survives colour-blindness, and it needs no animation. Keep the crack geometry subtle enough not to obscure a target at the centre of frame.
possibilities.prompt: First-person game frame. A cracked helmet visor overlay concentrated at the edges of the frame, hairline fractures radiating from one impact point, subtle warm rim glow at the breach. Damage is legible as material condition, not as a UI element. Muted environment behind the glass.

possibilities.title: Crowds that move as a fluid, not as agents
possibilities.tagline: Screen-space density field instead of per-agent simulation
possibilities.summary: Solve for density and velocity in screen space and derive the crowd from it, rather than simulating thousands of independent agents. The crowd gains coherent flow, obstacle avoidance and emergent eddies for a fraction of the cost, and it never needs per-agent bookkeeping.
possibilities.technique: Keep a coarse density and velocity texture. Move it with a semi-Lagrangian advection step, add a divergence-free projection pass, and inject avoidance force from a blurred obstacle mask. Sample the field when placing agents.
possibilities.rightsNote: Method is not protectable; implementations are. Treat upstream repositories as reference until licence is confirmed per file.
possibilities.buildNotes: A 128×128 field drives several thousand convincing agents. Projection is the step people skip, and it is the step that makes motion look like liquid rather than smoke.
possibilities.prompt: Technical plate: a crowd rendered as a screen-space density and velocity field. Streaklines integrated through the field, sampled particles as bright points, a density probe rail on the left. Dark ground, cool cyan to warm ember gradient along the flow.

possibilities.title: Characters readable as pure silhouette
possibilities.tagline: Designing poses for the smallest zoom level
possibilities.summary: Remove interior detail entirely and check the pose against a plain background. If the character is not identifiable as a solid shape at 24 pixels, no amount of texture work will save it. Negative space between limbs is a measurable constraint, not a matter of taste.
possibilities.technique: Fill the character as a single opaque shape and reduce to target size. Enforce a minimum gap of 2 px between limbs at the smallest zoom the game ever uses. Keep the centre of mass low and the stance wide.
possibilities.rightsNote: Study plate. Original character designs remain the property of their creators.
possibilities.buildNotes: A merged arm-and-torso mass is the most common failure. Fix it in the source pose rather than adding an outline shader at render time — an outline cannot recover articulation that is not there.
possibilities.prompt: Design study plate: three character poses rendered as flat black silhouettes on a dark field, one passing legibility at small size and one failing by merging into a single mass. Minimum negative space between limbs annotated at 2 pixels.

possibilities.title: Command palette as the only navigation
possibilities.tagline: One omnibar instead of a menu tree
possibilities.summary: Give the keyboard a single entry point that can reach every action, page and record, and let the menu bar become a fallback. Navigation stops being a tree the user has to learn and becomes a query they can improvise.
possibilities.technique: Fuzzy-match on every registered action and route, ranked by recency and prefix weight. Results carry an affordance glyph — enter to run, tab to select — so the keyboard path is discoverable without documentation.
possibilities.rightsNote: Interaction pattern is not licensable; the specific component implementation may be.
possibilities.buildNotes: Ranking is the whole product. Recency-weighted prefix matches beat pure fuzzy scoring almost every time. Show a keyboard shortcut on every result — a palette nobody discovers is a feature nobody uses.
possibilities.prompt: Interface plate: a command palette floating over a dimmed application. A single search field with typed input and a caret, results ranked with a bright left rule on the selected row, monospaced affordance glyphs on the right. Everything else pushed back in value.

possibilities.title: Breadcrumbs as a map, not a list of names
possibilities.tagline: Spatial position instead of a trail of ancestors
possibilities.summary: When the hierarchy is spatial, show the hierarchy spatially. A small plan view with the visited route drawn and the current node marked communicates depth, sibling count and backtracking in one glance, which a list of ancestor slugs never will.
possibilities.technique: Render a reduced plan: rooms as tone masses, connections as hairlines, the visited route as a single continuous stroke, the current position as concentric rings. Keep labels off the plan except for the current node.
possibilities.rightsNote: Pattern is free; map artwork is not. Keep the plan abstract rather than reproducing a real floorplan.
possibilities.buildNotes: The route stroke is what makes it a breadcrumb rather than a map. Without the travelled path the user learns where they are but not how they got there, and loses the ability to back out.
possibilities.prompt: Interface plate: an abstract architectural plan in cool low-contrast tone, a single ember stroke tracing the route taken, concentric rings marking the current room, nodes at each waypoint. A conventional breadcrumb bar ghosted below and struck through.

possibilities.title: Bento layouts with a deliberate density ramp
possibilities.tagline: One grid where emphasis steps down diagonally
possibilities.summary: Card grids usually shout everywhere at once. Put every cell on one grid and let a density ramp decide emphasis: one hero region, one secondary, a quieter band, then plain reference rows. Attention falls where the ramp says rather than where a border ends.
possibilities.technique: Assign each cell a tier. Tier sets fill opacity, border strength, type size and colour. Never mix tiers inside a single row. Reserve the highest tier for exactly one region per viewport.
possibilities.rightsNote: Layout logic is free to implement. Type, colour and imagery must each clear their own rights.
possibilities.buildNotes: The most common failure is a second hero cell. If two regions are both loud, the ramp is not a ramp and the eye has nowhere to land. Tier changes should be visible in the outline weight alone.
possibilities.prompt: Layout plate: a twelve-column bento wall on near-black. One wide ember-washed hero region, a tall count block beside it, a middle band of three, a denser grid below, and a borderless reference row. A density ramp annotated along the bottom.

possibilities.title: Gestures that hand off velocity to a spring
possibilities.tagline: A dismiss that knows how fast you meant it
possibilities.summary: Carry the gesture's velocity into the release, then let a critically-tuned spring finish the movement. Whether the sheet commits or returns is decided by crossing a threshold with momentum behind it, which is why it feels like an object rather than an animation.
possibilities.technique: Spring on position with initial velocity from the gesture. Scale rotation by drag distance. Once the threshold is crossed, stop tracking the finger and hand off entirely. Allow re-grab mid-flight.
possibilities.rightsNote: Physics approach is free. Any easing curve taken from a paid library is not.
possibilities.buildNotes: Position and velocity handoff is the whole trick; most implementations reset velocity on release and lose the feeling instantly. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by presenting a plain crossfade rather than disabling dismissal.
possibilities.prompt: Motion study plate: a bottom sheet captured mid-dismiss, rotated and offset with a dashed trail through the positions the gesture actually passed. Below it, a position-over-time curve with the release moment marked and the threshold line crossed.

possibilities.title: Negative-space marks
possibilities.tagline: A form that exists only where two shapes meet
possibilities.summary: Build a mark out of two solid shapes and let the gap between them be the figure. The identity reads as one form the viewer completes, which survives reproduction far better than a drawn symbol and needs no outline to hold it together.
possibilities.technique: Draw two solids, then find the shared boundary. That boundary is the mark. Test the reduction ladder — 48, 24, 16, 12 px — and the inverted version. One ink, flat, no gradients.
possibilities.rightsNote: A negative-space idea is not yours to trademark. Distinctiveness comes from the specific geometry; do not lift a competitor's construction and change the angles.
possibilities.buildNotes: The 12px test is the honest one. If the counter closes there, the mark is one that works in a deck and nowhere else — decide early whether that is acceptable.
possibilities.prompt: Mark construction plate: two solid wedges on a dark field with dashed construction lines, the shared diagonal called out as the actual mark. A reduction ladder at 48, 24, 16 and 12 pixels below, the 12 marked as a failure. An inverted one-ink proof to the side.

possibilities.title: One identity, four redraws
possibilities.tagline: A mark recomposed per placement instead of scaled
possibilities.summary: Ship a family of marks rather than one file. Recompose proportions for an app icon, a horizontal lockup, a stacked lockup and a one-ink version, bound by a small set of invariants so all four are recognisably the same identity.
possibilities.technique: Fix the invariants — apex angle, unit stroke, open counter — and let proportion, colour count and clear space vary per context. Recompute markspacing per lockup rather than inheriting a global value.
possibilities.rightsNote: Brand systems are among the most heavily policed marks. Register and clear before use in commerce.
possibilities.buildNotes: Colour count is the constraint that gets broken first. A brand with a fixed two-colour rule must define what happens when only one ink is available, and that answer has to exist before a designer needs it.
possibilities.prompt: Brand system plate: four placements of one mark — a single-colour app icon, a horizontal lockup, a stacked lockup with recomputed clear space, and a one-ink paper version. Construction lines showing the shared 2:1 apex angle.

possibilities.title: Generative marks with a bounded rule set
possibilities.tagline: A family that stays recognisable across every seed
possibilities.summary: Generate marks from a rule set rather than drawing them one at a time, and bound the parameters hard enough that every output reads as the same family. The output is unbounded; the identity is not.
possibilities.technique: Fix the structural invariants — a shared centre, equal bar lengths, open counter, square ends — and bound the variable ones, typically an angle range. Ship one fixed master alongside the generator.
possibilities.rightsNote: A generated output does not clear a mark for trademarking, and generative brand systems need a human check per output before public use.
possibilities.buildNotes: Test at thumbnail size before shipping the generator. If six seeds do not read as one identity at 24 pixels, the angle bound is too wide or the invariants too weak.
possibilities.prompt: Generative brand plate: a grid of six monogram instances produced by one rule set, ember and paper bars on a fixed centre at varying angles, the upper bound marked. Below, the same six reduced to 24 pixels as a family test.

possibilities.title: Duotone icon sets that survive being small
possibilities.tagline: Two inks carrying meaning, plus optical size correction
possibilities.summary: A single-weight outline set goes muddy at small sizes because every glyph renders at roughly the same visual mass. Give the set a second ink that carries state, and correct apparent weight per size so the row reads as even texture.
possibilities.technique: Build on a 24-unit grid with 2u padding. Provide a filled cut for 16px and progressively heavier strokes to 32px. Blur the whole set to 40% and check it reads as texture rather than as shapes.
possibilities.rightsNote: Icon sets are frequently derived from proprietary libraries. Confirm the licence of the master file, not just of the tool that exported it.
possibilities.buildNotes: Duotone is not decoration — the second ink must mean something. And duotone collapses to one ink when inverted, so the outline has to stand on its own. Check the inverted row.
possibilities.prompt: Icon design plate: two rows of five glyphs on dark. An outline row that goes grey at small size, and a duotone row with a cyan primary and a translucent secondary carrying state. Below, four optical size corrections of one glyph at increasing stroke weight, beside a 24-unit grid.

possibilities.title: Re-fit type to the measure
possibilities.tagline: A width axis instead of four separate cuts
possibilities.summary: When a headline does not fit the measure, most systems pick a different font or break the line. A variable width axis re-fits the same design to the space, preserving the voice and eliminating the drift that comes with swapping families.
possibilities.technique: Expose wdth on the variable axis and set textLength against the measure. Keep one optical size and one weight for the whole family so the letterforms stay related.
possibilities.rightsNote: Variable font licences vary enormously in what they allow — some restrict the number of static instances you may ship. Read the actual licence.
possibilities.buildNotes: Condensing to fit is usually better than dropping a line, but only within a sane range. Past roughly 15% condensation the letterforms start to hurt; at that point break the line instead.
possibilities.prompt: Typographic plate: the same short word set twice at different width axis positions on a near-black ground, with a measurement ruler beneath showing the fit. A condensed tabular numeral in ember. A line of body text demonstrating an overlong setting marked in warning orange.

possibilities.title: Optical size as a continuous axis
possibilities.tagline: The way printing has always done it
possibilities.summary: One typeface master re-drawn for the size it will land at. At 11 pixels terminals square off, spacing opens and thin joints return; at 144 pixels weight rises, contrast falls and curves smooth. Print has done this for centuries; screen type mostly has not.
possibilities.technique: Set the opsz axis from the computed font size and let the renderer interpolate. Do not round to discrete masters — the axis is continuous and intermediates are where most of the value is.
possibilities.rightsNote: Optical sizes ship in the font file. Confirm your font licence permits the axis and any derived masters.
possibilities.buildNotes: The payoff is largest in the small end, where a single master closes its counters. If your typeface has no optical axis, the second-best move is a separate small-size cut.
possibilities.prompt: Typography plate: the same phrase rendered three times at caption, text and display sizes over a faint grid, each annotated with what the optical size changes — terminals, spacing, weight, contrast. A comparison of single master and optical cut at small size.

possibilities.title: Cutting on the motion vector
possibilities.tagline: Velocity continuity instead of subject continuity
possibilities.summary: Match the screen-space displacement of a tracked feature across a cut and the seam disappears, even when subject, framing and palette all change. The perceived continuity comes from velocity, not from identity.
possibilities.technique: Track a feature through both shots. Plot per-frame displacement. Solve for the cut frame where displacement matches, then place the cut there. Velocity matching is cheaper and more forgiving than a full optical-flow solve.
possibilities.rightsNote: Technique is free. The footage is not, and cutting to another work's footage raises separate authorship questions.
possibilities.buildNotes: The cost is real: the cut can no longer be motivated by story, so the grade must carry whatever narrative the edit gave up. Do this for rhythm, not for plot.
possibilities.prompt: Edit study plate: two shots in frames, each with a tracked feature and its motion vector drawn, a dashed line spanning between the frames marking the matched displacement. Below, a per-frame displacement plot with the chosen cut frame marked.

possibilities.title: Kinetic type cut on transients
possibilities.tagline: The transient is the keyframe
possibilities.summary: Detected onsets, not beats, are what make type feel attached to music. Map onset energy onto weight and width and the word lands on the snare instead of near it. An easing curve applied to every word identically will always feel slightly late.
possibilities.technique: Run onset detection on the audio to get per-hit energy and position. Drive type size from energy, width from recovery after the hit. Re-derive on tempo change rather than storing absolute times.
possibilities.rightsNote: Method is free. The music is not, and syncing to a licensed track in published work needs the licence to permit it.
possibilities.buildNotes: BPM detection is not enough. Beats are regular; accents are not, and the difference between them is exactly what makes type feel locked. You need the audio, not the tempo map.
possibilities.prompt: Motion study plate: an audio waveform with detected transients marked and numbered above, and the same six transients applied to a word below as varying size and width, with attack traces between letters. A muted alternative approach shown alongside.

possibilities.title: Loops closed by periodicity
possibilities.tagline: Solve for the cycle instead of hiding the seam
possibilities.summary: Crossfading the ends of a loop doubles its length and leaves an audible dip. Making the state at t equal the state at the period removes the seam entirely — but it constrains the motion you can design, which is a design decision rather than a post-process.
possibilities.technique: Author the cycle so the final state equals the initial state, then validate numerically rather than by ear. For shaders, modulate the period rather than the offset. For audio, choose grains that overlap the boundary.
possibilities.rightsNote: Technique is free. Any loop built from someone else's recording inherits that recording's licence.
possibilities.buildNotes: Solving for the derivative rather than the value is what makes periodicity practical. A validator that compares endpoint state is worth more than an hour of ear-checking.
possibilities.prompt: Motion study plate: three panels comparing crossfade, ping-pong and periodicity, each showing the seam. Below, a cycle plotted as a curve whose start and end states are marked equal, with a dotted line showing the error being eliminated.

possibilities.title: Sustained beds from granular overlap
possibilities.tagline: Thousands of windowed grains instead of a loop
possibilities.summary: Take a short recording, window it into many small overlapping grains and scatter their pitch and timing. The result is a sustained texture that is not a loop, has no audible seam, and can be steered continuously.
possibilities.technique: Hann-window each grain, jitter pitch and start offset per grain, spread the grains across the stereo field and filter the result. Above roughly 30% overlap the bed stops sounding granular and starts sounding continuous.
possibilities.rightsNote: Grain a recording you do not own and you have made a derivative work. Verify the source licence before it becomes part of anything published.
possibilities.buildNotes: Hold drift above the noise floor or the bed collapses into mush — that is the one failure mode. Density below about 40% grains per second will sound granular in the wrong sense.
possibilities.prompt: Audio study plate: a short source waveform, a bed of overlapping grains with pitch and offset jitter, and below a resulting sustained texture with no seam at the loop point. Four labelled controls — density, jitter, drift, cutoff — plus a note that drift must stay above the noise floor.

possibilities.title: Timbre as a continuous parameter
possibilities.tagline: Interpolate the spectrum, not two oscillators
possibilities.summary: Blending two oscillators gives you two detuned things beating in the midrange. Interpolating one wavetable between two static spectra gives you a coherent timbre that passes through something worth hearing and stays stable under automation.
possibilities.technique: Build the tables so the midpoint is a good sound, not an average of two. Map one macro parameter to table mix and to several harmonic weights, so the timbre travels coherently rather than linearly.
possibilities.rightsNote: Synthesis method is free. Sampled wavetables are derivative works of their source recordings.
possibilities.buildNotes: The design work is in the tables, not the routing. If the midpoint sounds like nothing, the morph will feel like a switch with extra steps.
possibilities.prompt: Synthesis plate: two source spectra labelled hollow and reedy, then five morph stops between them with the midpoint marked as existing in no source table. Below, one macro parameter driving table mix, odd harmonic and even harmonic simultaneously.

possibilities.title: Edge-to-solid level of detail
possibilities.tagline: Crossfading geometry instead of swapping it
possibilities.summary: Draw the same geometry at every distance and shift the shading weight from edges to fill as the camera approaches. Nothing pops in, and you never have to author a separate far model — the transition is continuous because the geometry never changed.
possibilities.technique: Keep one mesh. Ramp a fill opacity and an edge opacity from a distance threshold, with the crossover positioned so both are legible. Cheapest LOD is the one you never had to build.
possibilities.rightsNote: Technique is free to implement. Any base mesh is the property of its author.
possibilities.buildNotes: A hard LOD swap draws the eye; a crossfade does not. The cost is one extra pass over triangles you were already drawing, which is usually cheaper than authoring and maintaining the second model.
possibilities.prompt: Technical plate: three frames of the same form at increasing distance — pure structure with no fill, edges with fill arriving, then solid surface with edges gone. Below, a plot of edge and fill opacity against distance with the crossover marked.

possibilities.title: Geometry as a distance function
possibilities.tagline: Editing the function instead of the model
possibilities.summary: Describe the scene as signed distance functions and raymarch it. There is no mesh, no texture and no vertex buffer — so the interesting edit is a change to a function, and shapes can be combined with smooth-min in ways a modeller would not attempt.
possibilities.technique: Define primitives as distance functions, combine with union, subtract and smooth-min, then sphere-trace with a bounded step count. One directional light term is enough to read form; add emissive accumulation as a separate pass.
possibilities.rightsNote: Signed distance functions as a technique are not protectable. Specific shader source in a repository is, and must be licence-checked before reuse.
possibilities.buildNotes: Step count is the whole performance story. A well-bounded SDF converges in far fewer steps than the maximum you budget for, so raising the cap costs nothing until it does — usually on the far plane.
possibilities.prompt: Render study plate: a raymarched scene of a sphere, a surrounding torus and an infinite floor with a glow pass, on a dark violet ground. A readout noting the step budget and that no mesh, texture or vertex buffer is involved.

possibilities.title: Append-only facts with disposable projections
possibilities.tagline: Never mutate history; rebuild the reads
possibilities.summary: Keep an append-only log of what happened and derive every read model from it. Projections are rebuildable and disposable; the log is the record. Two readers can want opposite things from the same facts without either compromising the other.
possibilities.technique: Append immutable events with a monotonic sequence. Build projections asynchronously and make them idempotent so replay is safe. Publish to the CMS through a projection, never by writing its tables directly.
possibilities.rightsNote: Architectural pattern is not protectable. Event schemas are yours; the code that reads them is not, if you copied it.
possibilities.buildNotes: The schema is forever and the projections are disposable. Decide that up front or you will end up with a projection that something else has started depending on, which is the worst of both worlds.
possibilities.prompt: Architecture plate: an append-only event log on the left feeding two separate projections on the right — a coverage index and a licence ledger — each labelled rebuildable. Annotated with the trade-offs: audit trail gained, projection cost paid, event schema permanent.

possibilities.title: Capabilities declared, not assumed
possibilities.tagline: A missing capability is a value, not an exception
possibilities.summary: Extensions should ask for what they need and adapt to what the host can honour. A feature the host cannot support is removed from the surface entirely, so it can never be half-broken — the alternative is a UI that renders a control which fails when pressed.
possibilities.technique: Declare required, optional and declined capabilities separately. For each optional capability provide a working fallback, not a disabled control. Test the degraded configuration as a first-class target.
possibilities.rightsNote: Pattern is free. Plugin permission models are worth reviewing before adopting any specific registry.
possibilities.buildNotes: Installed is not supported. The failure mode to avoid is a plugin that renders its full feature set against a host that quietly does not honour half of it.
possibilities.prompt: Architecture plate: a host advertising storage, database, auth and admin capabilities, connected to two deployment targets that answer differently. Below, the plugin's declaration list separating required, optional and declined capabilities with the fallback behaviour for each.

possibilities.title: Content-addressed asset storage
possibilities.tagline: The name is the proof
possibilities.summary: Identify assets by hashing their bytes. Dedupe becomes exact, a provenance chain is just a list of addresses, and originals are immutable by construction because a derived file necessarily gets a different address. A verifier can recompute the whole chain offline.
possibilities.technique: Hash on ingest and store under the hash. Record the parent address for every derivative and never overwrite a parent. Resolve names to addresses at the edge, so a filename can change without moving a byte.
possibilities.rightsNote: Technique is standard and freely implementable. The hashes, paths and filenames inside are content and carry their own provenance obligations.
possibilities.buildNotes: This is what makes a licence correction cheap: rewrite the record, never the bytes. It also means the same asset found in two places is one catalogue entry with two sources, which is exactly what option-space coverage needs.
possibilities.prompt: Systems plate: source bytes entering a hash, the hash as identity, then four derivatives fanning out — one deduplicated, two derived with parent records, and one that shares a filename with different bytes. Immutable originals and verifiable chains annotated below.

possibilities.title: Confidence rendered as content
possibilities.tagline: Never let a weak claim read as a strong one
possibilities.summary: An AI system that states weak inferences as plainly as strong ones has miscalibrated its output. Show support counts inline, texture the uncertain parts rather than only colouring them, and let every claim be traced to the sources behind it.
possibilities.technique: Attach a support count to each claim and render it at the point of the claim. Encode uncertainty in texture and weight as well as colour so it survives greyscale and colour-blindness. Link every claim to its source list.
possibilities.rightsNote: Presentation patterns are free, but never let an uncertainty display imply a licence or provenance conclusion it has not actually verified.
possibilities.buildNotes: Keep machine evidence separate from editorial judgement in the data model too, not only in the interface — otherwise a well-designed uncertainty display will be fed confident nonsense.
possibilities.prompt: Interface plate: a generated answer where strong clauses are set plainly and a weak clause is filled with diagonal hatching, outlined dashed and annotated with its support count. Below, coverage and novelty plotted as bars, and a note that uncertainty never uses colour alone.

possibilities.title: A mark that is one weight at every size
possibilities.tagline: Fixed stroke, scaling geometry, nothing else to specify
possibilities.summary: Build the mark from a single stroke weight and let everything else scale. The identity becomes a rule rather than a drawing: the same mark at a favicon and on a hoarding is recognisably the same mark, and a third party can reproduce it from one number. The trade is apparent weight — a fixed stroke looks heavier as it shrinks — which you either accept or correct deliberately at named sizes.
possibilities.technique: Draw once at a reference size with a single stroke weight and no optical compensation. Then produce a reduction ladder: the same geometry at 64, 44 and 28px with the weight unchanged, and a second ladder where you reduce the weight by one unit below 40px and open the gaps by one unit to match. Choose the ladder, not the file.
possibilities.rightsNote: The rule is free to use and the drawing is not. A monoline construction is a technique; the particular geometry, ratios and angles are somebody's, and distinctiveness comes from the specifics you chose, not from the constraint you followed.
possibilities.buildNotes: One weight is checkable with a ruler and two weights is a judgement you have to defend every time. Ship the one-weight version as the default and document the ladder as an exception list, so the exception is the visible part.
possibilities.prompt: Mark construction plate on a dark ground: a large monoline glyph drawn at reference size with a measurement bracket calling out the single stroke weight, a reduction ladder at 64, 44 and 28 pixels below it with the weight held constant, and a second ladder with the weight and the gaps both reduced. Mono annotations, one accent, no gradients.

possibilities.title: A lettermark whose hole is the mark
possibilities.tagline: Extract the counter of a letter and fill it
possibilities.summary: Take a single letter, isolate its counter — the enclosed negative shape — and use that shape alone as the mark. The letter is the source, not the artwork: the identity is a silhouette derived from one piece of type, which gives it a recognisable lineage without carrying any of the wordmark's weight. It only works if the counter is generous enough to survive as a shape on its own.
possibilities.technique: Set the letter at the weight and optical size you will use, trace the counter exactly, then clear it and fill it as a solid. Test the extracted shape alone at 88, 48, 29 and 15px. Two radii meeting at a point hold; two radii meeting smoothly do not, because the point is what the eye was reading.
possibilities.rightsNote: Letterforms in most jurisdictions are not copyrightable, but that is not the same as being free to ship. Check the licence on any typeface you draw the counter from, and do not extend a competitor's specific counter into your own identity.
possibilities.buildNotes: A counter narrower than the stroke closes solid at small sizes and stops being a mark at all. Decide early whether you can live with a mark that only works above 30px, because that decision constrains every container it will ever sit in.
possibilities.prompt: Lettermark construction plate: a heavy serif letter drawn in outline with its counter called out in a dashed accent, and beside it the counter lifted out and filled as a solid ember shape. Below, a reduction ladder of the extracted counter alone at 88, 48, 29 and a failing 15 pixels, with the 15 marked as a failure. Mono annotations on a dark ground.

possibilities.title: A mark you can rebuild from a division rule
possibilities.tagline: Three by three, and nothing drawn that is not already on the grid
possibilities.summary: Define a square divided into ninths, then take the mark from a subset of those divisions. The value is not the shape — it is that the shape is a consequence, so anybody who has the rule can redraw the mark exactly, a contractor can extend it without a handover document, and a future designer cannot accidentally drift it by nudging one edge.
possibilities.technique: Fix the container as a square and the division as 3 × 3, then choose cells. Keep every edge of every drawn shape on a division line. Above 32px the cell pattern can be shown; below it, redraw the silhouette the cells describe, because the gaps close first.
possibilities.rightsNote: Division systems are older than any of us and are not protectable as such. What is yours is the specific subset you chose, so do not reproduce a competitor's cell selection and describe it as systematic.
possibilities.buildNotes: The rule is the deliverable and the drawing is an instance of it — ship the rule. The moment the rule is the drawing, every future revision becomes an argument about whether the drift was intentional.
possibilities.prompt: Mark construction plate: a large square subdivided into a three by three grid, three cells filled to form a diagonal mark, the subdivision drawn in dashed cyan over a fine grid, and below a reduction ladder of the mark alone at 144, 79, 43 and a failing 23 pixels. Mono annotations, one accent, dark ground.

possibilities.title: A wordmark whose only decision is the space
possibilities.tagline: Tracking specified as a number, gaps applied optically
possibilities.summary: Some identities have no symbol at all — the word itself is the mark, and the only thing that makes it a wordmark rather than default interface type is the space between the letters. Specify the tracking as a number so it can be set consistently, then correct it optically per gap so it survives being used at sizes nobody checked.
possibilities.technique: Set the word in one weight at one size with negative tracking. Then measure the gaps between stems and set each individually: round-sided letters need less air than flat-sided ones, and a letter with a leg needs less again. Ship the per-gap values, not the global number, because the global number is what gets lost in a redesign.
possibilities.rightsNote: Trademark distinctiveness in a wordmark comes from the specific letterforms and the specific spacing arrangement. A tracking value is not protectable and copying it is not infringement — but arriving at the same word with the same spacing by coincidence is a real legal question, not a design one.
possibilities.buildNotes: Text zoom breaks wordmarks before anything else does. If the identity depends on -2 units of tracking, it needs a second setting for large text sizes, and that second setting needs testing rather than assuming.
possibilities.prompt: Wordmark plate on a dark ground: a large tracked-out wordmark with a baseline rule and the tracking value called out in cyan, three stacked variants below showing uniform tracking, tracking dropped and tracking specified, and a final diagram showing per-gap values annotated in ember on six letters. Mono annotations, one accent.

possibilities.title: A mark redrawn for its largest size, not scaled to it
possibilities.tagline: Master at 48px, every other size drawn from it
possibilities.summary: A vector file scaled to poster size multiplies its stroke weight with its geometry, so the mark arrives heavier than it was drawn and the counters arrive softer. Treat every size as its own drawing session: nominate one master size, author the weight at each size, and open the counters back up as the mark grows.
possibilities.technique: Nominate the 48px square as the master. Produce the other sizes as redraws with an authored weight rather than as scaled copies — at 6× the stroke can drop from four units to under two and the counters come back. Record the size list in the asset itself so nobody has to guess which file is the master.
possibilities.rightsNote: No rights question in the technique. The rights question is the one you create by shipping nine near-identical files and calling them one logo: that is a maintenance liability, not a legal one.
possibilities.buildNotes: If you cannot name the size list, you do not have a master — you have a directory. The list is short (favicon, 48, and the largest physical print) and it is the only thing that keeps a mark consistent across a brand's lifetime.
possibilities.prompt: Mark plate on a dark ground: two squares side by side, the left holding a mark scaled six times with visibly heavy joints labelled as a failure, the right holding the same geometry redrawn with an authored weight and open counters, plus a row of three delivery sizes below with the master called out. Mono annotations, one accent.

possibilities.title: A mark defined by the angle cut across its stroke
possibilities.tagline: One angle, one weight, one radius — and a family that falls out of it
possibilities.summary: Draw the mark as a stroked arc and cut the terminals at an angle rather than shaping them. The angle is the identity, and because it scales with the stroke it survives reduction where a bespoke terminal shape does not. The useful consequence is a family: one arc and one cut produce the whole set of sizes and radii the brand needs.
possibilities.technique: Set the cap angle as a single number — 45° is a defensible default — and apply it to both ends. Test 0° (a default cap, not a mark), 90° (a cut pipe) and 22.5° (too close to 0° to hold). Then derive the family by changing only the radius and the stroke weight, never the angle.
possibilities.rightsNote: The angle-and-radius system is a technique. A competitor's specific arc, angle and radius combination is a drawing, and the combination can be distinctive — check before adopting one you found rather than invented.
possibilities.buildNotes: Below about 14px the cut stops being visible and the mark becomes an arc, which is a different mark. Either accept a floor of 16px on the identity, or state in advance which smaller cut replaces it.
possibilities.prompt: Mark construction plate on a dark ground: four stroked arcs of the same radius showing terminal cuts at 0, 45, 90 and 22.5 degrees, the 45 degree version drawn in paper white with its cut faces filled in ember, plus a small reduction ladder at 40, 24 and 12 pixels. Mono annotations, one accent, no gradients.

possibilities.title: An icon family held together by a check, not a guideline
possibilities.tagline: One weight, one cap height, one radius — enforced in the build
possibilities.summary: A family of marks is a constraint, and the failure is always the same: somebody adds a sixth icon later at a different weight with a different corner radius. Write the constraint as four machine-checkable numbers — stroke weight, rendered height, permitted radii, and a ban on scale() in the source — and enforce them in the build. A guideline nobody runs is not a constraint.
possibilities.technique: Write the constraint as assertions: stroke-width equals one value, rendered height equals one value within a tolerance, corner radius is in a permitted set, and no path uses scale(). Enforce them where the icons are built, not in a document. Every icon shares one cap height and one terminal angle, so optical tops align even when the geometry does not.
possibilities.rightsNote: No rights question in the constraint. The rights question arrives when a family member is lifted from another system's icon set to fill a gap — at which point it is a drawing you did not draw.
possibilities.buildNotes: The gate is the deliverable and the icons are the instance of it, exactly as with the grid mark. Without the gate you get one wrong icon in every nine, and the wrong one is always the one somebody added in a hurry.
possibilities.prompt: Icon family plate on a dark ground: five line icons — circle, square, triangle, chevron, rounded square — drawn on one stroke weight with dashed optical-top and baseline rules in cyan, and below a sixth icon visibly off-weight with an ember overlay marking the drift, followed by four assertion lines. Mono annotations, one accent.

possibilities.title: A lockup shipped as a relationship, not as a file
possibilities.tagline: Mark and wordmark on a shared axis, with a stated gap
possibilities.summary: The mark-and-wordmark combination is where most identity systems are actually used, and it is the artefact most often exported wrongly — as one flattened file, at one width, with a gap somebody typed as a percentage. Ship the relationship: a shared optical axis, a gap stated in units of the mark's own width, and a horizontal, stacked and symbol-only variant for the three widths that matter.
possibilities.technique: Set the master lockup with the mark's cap height as the unit, the gap as a fixed number of those units, and the wordmark cap height as a stated fraction. Derive the horizontal, stacked and symbol-only variants by re-locking the same parts. Do not export the variants as scaled copies, and do not leave the gap as a percentage — a percentage gap closes as the mark shrinks.
possibilities.rightsNote: No rights question in the lockup rule. There is one in the wordmark itself, and in any mark you adopted from a competitor's lockup rather than drew.
possibilities.buildNotes: Three lockups is the whole deliverable and all three have to be drawn, because a lockup is not a responsive layout. Above 180px the horizontal version, above 96px the stacked version, and below that the mark alone — with the thresholds stated so somebody else can apply them.
possibilities.prompt: Lockup plate on a dark ground: a large horizontal mark-and-wordmark lockup on a paper white field with the optical axis and gap called out in cyan, a smaller one at the same relationship, a third with a percentage gap closing and marked in amber, and below three container variants — horizontal, stacked and symbol only. Mono annotations, one accent.

possibilities.title: A reversed mark that is a second drawing, not a colour swap
possibilities.tagline: Two files, two weights, one geometry
possibilities.summary: Light ink on a dark ground spreads, so the same stroke reads heavier and a tight counter reads closed. The reversed mark therefore needs its own authored weight and its own opened counters — measured, not estimated. Shipping one file called "the logo" and letting somebody recolour it in a hurry is how a brand ends up with a reversed version nobody approved.
possibilities.technique: Draw the geometry once. Then draw it twice: once dark on light at the authored weight, once light on dark with the weight reduced by roughly 8 to 12 percent and the tightest counter opened by the same fraction. Place them side by side at the same size and measure the apparent difference before shipping.
possibilities.rightsNote: No rights question in the method. There is one in shipping a competitor's reversed version, which is a distinct drawing rather than a colour change and is treated as such.
possibilities.buildNotes: Both files belong in the asset library with the same name and a reversed suffix, so the reversed one is what a designer reaches for rather than something they rebuild in the tool they happen to have open.
possibilities.prompt: Mark plate on a dark ground: a positive proof in dark ink on a paper white tile and a reversed proof in light ink on a near-black tile with the weight visibly reduced, then a second pair below using the same weight in both, the reversed one marked in amber as reading heavier. Mono annotations, one accent.

possibilities.title: A symbol sized for the containers it will live in
possibilities.tagline: Clearspace as a ratio of the mark, not as nine exported crops
possibilities.summary: A symbol on its own is not a deliverable — a symbol on a square app tile, on a wide banner and on a tall avatar is three different drawings, because proportional shrinking closes the counters and filling the container kills the clearspace. State the clearspace as a ratio of the mark's own width, cap the mark at a percentage of each container, and draw the three containers rather than exporting crops of one.
possibilities.technique: Declare clearspace as a fraction of the mark's own width — a quarter is a defensible default — and apply it on every side of every container. Cap the mark at 50 percent of a square tile, 42 percent of a tall container's width, and never scale a container drawing proportionally: redraw it, or let the mark lose weight while the geometry holds.
possibilities.rightsNote: No rights question in the ratio. There is one in the container artwork itself if it is a third party's photograph rather than a flat field — which is also why flat fields are the safer default.
possibilities.buildNotes: A new container shape is a new drawing, not a crop. Agree that up front, because every brand that has not agreed it up front ends up with a symbol stretched onto a surface it was never drawn for.
possibilities.prompt: Symbol plate on a dark ground: three paper white containers — a rounded square app tile, a wide banner and a tall avatar — each holding the same mark at a stated maximum width, and two wrong versions below, one filled to the edges and one proportionally shrunk with closed counters, both marked in amber. Mono annotations, one accent.

collections.title: Replacing the obvious
collections.tagline: Default solutions and the distinct alternatives to them
collections.summary: Most interface and game problems get solved the same way every time. Each entry here is a materially different way to answer a question you already know the default answer to.

collections.title: Procedural without an engine
collections.tagline: Simulation and geometry written as maths, not imported as a plugin
collections.summary: Approaches where the interesting part is the maths and the dependency budget is zero. Often cheaper, often smaller, occasionally the only thing that fits the constraint.

collections.title: The system is the artwork
collections.tagline: Bounded rules that produce a recognisable family
collections.summary: Marks, sets and sounds generated from a rule set rather than drawn individually. The output varies; the identity does not. The hard part is always the bound.

collections.title: Seams
collections.tagline: Problems that live entirely at a boundary
collections.summary: Loop points, edit points, cut points, boundaries between two colours. Each of these is a place where an artefact hides, and each becomes tractable once you solve for the right quantity.

sections.title: Field guide
sections.description: Opening sentence shown under the catalogue wall's title. Read by src/pages/index.astro via src/lib/site-shell.ts.

children.text: Each plate is one distinct possibility rather than one file. Drill in for the technique, the build notes, a prompt scaffold and the rights.

pages.title: What this is
pages.summary: A catalogue of distinct creative and technical possibilities, with representative examples and their provenance.

children.text: Possibilities, not files
Five thousand logo files are not five thousand useful things to look at. They might demonstrate forty materially different treatments. This catalogue is built around the forty.

Every entry is a possibility — a specific idea, technique, pattern or mechanic that can be recreated. Each one carries representative examples, and every example states where it came from and what its rights actually are.
Three things worth knowing
Possibility is not permission

Learning that a treatment exists says nothing about whether you may copy the asset that demonstrated it. Rights are tracked per example, never per possibility, and reference-only material is never presented as cleared.
Examples state their origin

Upstream means shown directly from discovered material. Derived means a safe preview produced from it. Generated means newly made to demonstrate a known possibility. The three are never mixed in a row.
Machine evidence and editorial judgement stay apart
Coverage, novelty and support counts are observations. Editorial curation is a human decision. They can influence ranking and they never overwrite each other.
What is here now

The catalogue is seeded with generated plates and their reference material. Upstream examples arrive through the discovery engine, which crawls permitted sources and publishes through a documented contract. Where a count is not yet machine-verified it reads zero rather than being estimated.

pages.title: Licensing and rights
pages.summary: How rights are classified, what each status means, and what this catalogue will never claim for you.

children.text: The statuses
Cleared
A licence was read from the source itself and recorded, and that licence permits the use being made of it. Cleared applies to a specific example, never to a possibility in the abstract.
Attribution required
Use is permitted provided the recorded attribution is reproduced. The attribution text is stored with the example so it travels with the asset.
Review required

Something was detected but not understood well enough to rely on: a licence file that contradicts the repository, a licence that changed at a tag, a non-commercial or share-alike restriction whose scope is unclear.
Reference only
No licence was found, or the material is explicitly not licensed for reuse. The example is preserved because it demonstrates a real possibility. That is the entire extent of its permission.
What this will not do

Repository licence metadata is treated as a hint, never as the sole authority. Unknown material is never described as cleared. Transforming an asset with an AI tool does not clear it. Possibility discovery does not grant rights to the source asset, and none of the plates here are a substitute for reading a licence.
If something here is wrong

Corrections are auditable and take effect on the record rather than on the asset. Content addressing means a licence can be corrected without touching the bytes, and the previous classification is kept rather than overwritten.

Every drill-in carries a report form that takes the words you would use rather than this catalogue's internal classifications. Report the licence, the attribution, a dead source, an asset that should not be handed over, an infringement claim, or simply that you made the work and do not want it here. You do not need to know which of those the catalogue will call it.
Taking something down

A report that says a rights claim is open, or that the work should not be surfaced at all, withdraws the download the moment it is filed. The file stops being served at its address immediately; the entry leaves the public catalogue if the report is about the whole entry. Nothing is deleted, and no account or proof of authorship is needed for the request to be honoured first and argued about afterwards.

The source, the licence evidence, the commit and the content hash stay on the record, because they are what a correction is made from and what proves what was served. What stops is the handover. The same request also excludes the source from future ingestion, so a later crawl cannot put it back: an exclusion is a durable record, not a box somebody ticks. If one example has to go, the possibility it demonstrated stays, and another example is chosen to represent it.

Every change says which field moved, what it held before, what it holds now, and why, and that trail is kept with the record. Nothing about a disputed payload stays publicly served while it is examined.

pages.title: Run it locally
pages.summary: Serve the catalogue locally, publish new possibilities into it with a hunt, and run the checks that tell you whether either worked.

children.text: The catalogue and the hunt engine are two systems with a documented boundary, and this is the whole of the local loop. The engine crawls, reads licences and groups candidates into possibilities; the catalogue decides what the public sees.
Serve the catalogue
Node 22 or newer, then:

The wall is on port 4321 and the EmDash admin at /_emdash/admin. The first run applies pending migrations and the seed schema. A fresh database has no content until you ask for the demo catalogue, which is one more request:
That endpoint creates a local development admin and refuses to run outside the dev server. It is not how production is set up, and it is not an authentication path anyone can reach in public.
Publish new possibilities

A hunt takes a brief, crawls permitted sources, reads the licence beside each asset rather than the repository's, and groups candidates into possibilities. It writes a payload to disk; it does not write to the CMS. The four commands below crawl, reconcile into the catalogue, and then prove the catalogue matches the payload. Without a GitHub token the search API allows ten requests a minute, which is enough to try it and slow enough to be unpleasant; gh auth token lifts it.

body.code:
export GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token)
npm run hunt -- sfx.json
npm run hunt:sync
npm run hunt:verify

children.text: What a hunt does not do

A crawl never decides what the public catalogue shows. Machine entries arrive as drafts at the bottom of the wall, and promoting one is a person's decision made in the admin. The check below fails if a draft has leaked onto the public wall.
Check it honestly

The gate for a change needs no server: it typechecks, validates the seed, measures every plate and runs the tests. The full gate adds the four checks that can only be made against a running site — that the catalogue really is served by EmDash, that an edit made in the admin reaches a reader and is then put back, that the masthead really is the CMS menu, and the visual pass. All of it is local: there are no hosted CI checks, and none are planned.

body.code:
npm run verify
npm run verify:full

children.text: The catalogue is also a read-only JSON contract at /api/catalogue.json, so a script can ask it a question without scraping HTML. It serves published entries only, needs no token, and keeps null distinct from zero.

body.code:
npm run catalogue -- summary
npm run catalogue -- search "seam"
npm run catalogue -- rights
